title: Signs Your AC Compressor Is Failing
h1: What Are the Signs an AC Compressor Is Failing?
description: Warm air, loud starts, tripped breakers and a humming outdoor unit can all point to a failing AC compressor. Here is what to watch for and what to do next.
quick_answer: The most common signs of a failing AC compressor are warm air from the vents, grinding or rattling from the outdoor unit, a breaker that keeps tripping, an outdoor unit that hums or clicks but never starts, and cooling that gets weaker over the season. Many of these can also come from cheaper parts, so get it diagnosed before assuming the worst.
body:
The compressor is the pump inside your outdoor unit that moves refrigerant through the system. When it starts to fail, you usually notice weaker cooling first, then noises, then electrical trouble. Catching it early can mean the difference between replacing a small part and replacing the whole outdoor unit.

What does a failing compressor sound like?

A healthy compressor makes a steady, low hum. Listen near the outdoor unit while the system starts up and runs for a few minutes. These sounds are worth a service call:

  • Grinding or scraping, which can point to worn internal parts.
  • Rattling or banging that starts when the compressor kicks on.
  • A loud clunk at startup or shutdown that wasn't there before.
  • High-pitched squealing or hissing, which can come from high internal pressure or a refrigerant leak.
  • Repeated clicking with no startup, often an electrical problem at the compressor.

Not every rattle means the compressor is done. Loose panels, a bent fan blade or debris inside the cabinet can make similar noises, which is why a technician checks the whole unit before blaming the compressor.

What are the other warning signs?

Warm or barely cool air

If the indoor blower is running but the air from the registers feels close to room temperature, the compressor may not be running or may not be building enough pressure. Low refrigerant, a dirty outdoor coil and a failed capacitor cause the same symptom, so this one needs testing.

The breaker keeps tripping

A compressor that's struggling to start pulls a lot of current. If the AC breaker trips again after you reset it once, leave it off. Resetting a breaker over and over can damage the compressor motor and the wiring, and it's a sign something needs a proper electrical check.

The outdoor unit hums but the compressor won't start

Sometimes the fan spins and you hear a hum, but cooling never kicks in. This "hard start" problem is often a weak capacitor or a worn contactor, both of which are much cheaper fixes than a compressor. Left alone, though, repeated hard starts wear the compressor down.

Short cycling

If the system turns on, runs for a minute or two, then shuts off and repeats, the compressor may be overheating and tripping its internal safety. Dirty coils, low refrigerant and thermostat problems also cause short cycling.

Higher bills and longer run times

A compressor losing efficiency runs longer to do the same job. If your summer bill jumps and the house never quite reaches the setpoint, the compressor is one of the things to check.

Oily spots or ice on the lines

Oil residue around the refrigerant lines or fittings can mean a leak. Ice on the larger copper line or the indoor coil often points to low refrigerant or poor airflow, both of which make the compressor work harder.

Why do compressors fail early?

Most compressors don't just wear out on their own. Something else in the system usually pushes them past their limits:

  • Dirty outdoor coils that can't shed heat, so pressures and temperatures climb.
  • Low refrigerant from a leak, which can overheat the compressor.
  • Clogged filters or blocked returns that starve the indoor coil of airflow.
  • Electrical wear in capacitors and contactors that makes every start harder.
  • Corrosion on coils and electrical connections, common on coastal homes where salt air reaches the outdoor unit.

Hot inland summers add to the load. A unit in an inland neighborhood can run for most of the afternoon in July and August, so small problems show up faster there.

What should you do if you suspect the compressor?

Start with the simple checks you can safely do yourself:

  1. Make sure the thermostat is set to cool and a few degrees below room temperature.
  2. Replace the air filter if it's dirty.
  3. Clear leaves, weeds and stored items from around the outdoor unit.
  4. Check that the AC breaker is on. If it trips again after one reset, leave it off.

Beyond that, stop. Testing capacitors, checking refrigerant pressures and measuring compressor windings involves high voltage and refrigerant, which is work for a trained technician. Opening the electrical panel on the unit is not a safe DIY job.

Repair or replace if the compressor is bad?

If the problem turns out to be a capacitor, contactor or a refrigerant leak that can be repaired, you're usually looking at a repair. If the compressor itself has failed, the decision depends on the age of the system, its overall condition and what refrigerant it uses. On an older system, a compressor replacement can cost enough that putting the money toward a new, more efficient unit makes more sense.

A technician can lay out both options with real numbers for your home. You can learn more about our air conditioning repair and replacement service, and we provide a free estimate on replacements so you can compare before deciding.

How do you keep a compressor healthy?

An annual tune-up before summer is the best protection. A technician cleans the outdoor coil, checks refrigerant levels, tests the capacitor and contactor, and tightens electrical connections. Between visits, change your filter on schedule and keep a couple of feet of clear space around the outdoor unit. Those habits keep pressures and temperatures where they belong and give the compressor its best shot at a long life.
faqs: Can a failing AC compressor be repaired?

Sometimes. Many problems that look like compressor failure are really a bad capacitor, contactor or a refrigerant leak, and those can be repaired. If the compressor motor or internal parts have failed, it usually has to be replaced, and on an older system replacing the whole outdoor unit may be the better value.
Is it safe to keep running my AC with a bad compressor?

It is better not to. Running a struggling compressor can trip breakers, overheat wiring and turn a smaller repair into a bigger one. If you hear grinding, smell burning or the breaker keeps tripping, shut the system off at the thermostat and have it checked.
How long does an AC compressor last?

A well-maintained compressor often lasts as long as the rest of the outdoor unit. Dirty coils, low refrigerant, poor airflow and electrical wear are what shorten its life, so regular maintenance makes a real difference.
Why does my outdoor unit hum but not start?

A humming outdoor unit that never starts cooling often has a weak capacitor or a stuck contactor. Shut the system off and call for service, because repeated failed starts put extra strain on the compressor.
